query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A combined in situ thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and high-temperature XRD method will enable simultaneous measurement of real-time oxidation kinetics and phase evolution in multicomponent alloys exposed to elevated temperatures, thereby capturing transient oxidation products that are missed by conventional ex situ measurements.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy or multi-element alloy in the as-cast or as-sintered condition, with a relatively uniform bulk composition and microstructure.
generation.intervention: Place the alloy in a high-temperature chamber equipped with both thermogravimetric and XRD capabilities to continuously record mass changes and diffraction patterns during controlled heating and oxidizing conditions.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures representative of the service environment (e.g., 600–1200 °C), with a chosen oxidizing atmosphere (air or controlled O2 partial pressure).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of transient oxides and the evolution of stable phases, directly observed by XRD in real-time, correlated to TGA-based mass gains/losses.
generation.mechanism: In situ data collection reveals the kinetics and sequential phase transformations during oxidation and identifies short-lived oxide species that form and subsequently transform at high temperature, enabling a direct link between microstructural evolution and weight changes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Transitory oxide phases and changes in the underlying alloy structure will be directly observed in real time, correlating precisely with mass changes from TGA. This evidence will confirm distinct oxidation stages that are otherwise obscured in purely ex situ or mass-only measurements.
generation.baseline: Conventional TGA combined with ex situ XRD captures only endpoint measurements and may miss important transformations or short-lived intermediate oxides during high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: Requires specialized equipment (i.e., high-temperature XRD cell coupled with TGA) and carefully controlled atmosphere; sample geometries or compositions that significantly attenuate or scatter the X-ray signal may be challenging to analyze.
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature ranges and oxide identification may vary among different alloy compositions, and the prevalence of transient phases depends on specific element interactions and partial pressures of reactive gases.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare results from standard TGA/ex situ XRD testing with in situ TGA/XRD measurements performed under the same heating schedule and atmosphere. If both experiments identify the same final phases but the in situ experiment reveals additional transient phases and distinct reaction stages, it supports the hypothesis.
measurements: Time-resolved TGA for continuous mass change
Post-exposure microstructure characterization via ex situ XRD or SEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Should the in situ method fail to reveal different or intermediate phases and show the same results as final ex situ characterization, then the hypothesis that combined in situ TGA/XRD offers unique insight into transient oxide formation would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. decision.trend: In the earlier literature on high-temperature alloys, the main approach to quantifying oxidation kinetics is to measure weight gain or loss at high temperature (thermogravimetric analysis, or TGA), often combined with post-exposure characterization of scale morphology and phase evolution by XRD or microstructural examination. Studies on refractory high-entropy alloys demonstrate that TGA at elevated temperature for fixed durations is a common baseline. Most also rely on ex situ XRD to identify phase changes before and after exposure. More recent investigations have begun using in situ methods such as high-temperature XRD measurements to track evolving crystal structure in real time. While TGA and ex situ XRD confirm bulk oxidation kinetics and final phases, direct in situ identification of intermediate and transient phases under reactive conditions remains comparatively unexplored.
decision.unsolved: A major challenge is capturing real-time phase transformations and transient oxide formation at high temperatures. Conventional TGA tracks net mass changes but does not distinguish which phases are emerging or dissolving, while ex situ XRD can miss key transitions that occur transiently or at high growth rates. Consequently, there is a gap in time-resolved in situ approaches that can link precise oxidation kinetics to corresponding phase evolution.
decision.lever: Perform in situ TGA coupled with synchrotron or high-temperature XRD under controlled atmosphere to measure real-time mass change and phase evolution simultaneously in the temperature range of interest
decision.why: Building on the established use of TGA and ex situ XRD for high-temperature oxidation studies, coupling a thermogravimetric balance with an in situ XRD system under elevated temperatures and controlled atmospheres would enable direct correlation between oxidation kinetics and evolving phase stability. This approach addresses the remaining challenge of capturing transient phases and their formation/dissolution dynamics, providing deeper mechanistic insight than traditional end-point measurements.
